topic: Using the rational root theorem to find zeros
subtitle: Using the rational root theorem to find zeros

problems.desc: Rubric for the list of possible rational zeros. The numerator must divide the constant term six and the denominator must divide the leading coefficient one, so the complete list is plus and minus one, two, three and six. Full credit requires all eight values with both signs. Deduct for a list that omits the negatives, which is the usual omission, and for any value that is not a divisor of six.

Rubric for the list of possible rational zeros. Numerators must divide the constant term four, giving one, two and four; denominators must divide the leading coefficient three, giving one and three. The complete list is therefore plus and minus one, two, four, one third, two thirds and four thirds. Full credit requires the fractional candidates as well as the whole-number ones, since dropping them is the error this problem is built to expose.

Rubric for the written conclusion. The answer must name two as the zero and give the reason: substituting it made the polynomial equal zero, while substituting four gave a non-zero value, and a number is a zero exactly when the polynomial evaluates to zero there. Accept wording that says four is not a zero because the value was not zero. No credit for naming two with no reference to the values computed above.

Rubric for the written explanation. A full-credit answer says the theorem only ever proposes RATIONAL numbers, so a zero that is not rational can never appear on its candidate list, and the remaining two zeros here are not real at all. It should add that the theorem is a first step that reduces the degree, after which the leftover quadratic is handled by the quadratic formula. Accept an answer that says the candidate list is finite and made of fractions built from the constant and leading coefficients. No credit for restating the two remaining zeros with no comment on why the theorem missed them.
